newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House revamps major education law for disabled.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House revamps major education law for disabled.

text.p: The House Tuesday voted to overhaul a far-reaching law guaranteeing free public education to more than five million disabled children nationwide, giving schools new flexibility and parents more input.

The overwhelming 420-3 bipartisan vote to rewrite the 1975 Individuals with Disabilities Education Act was the culmination of months of intense negotiations between the White House and both parties in Congress.

The compromise, which the Senate will vote on Wednesday, does not alter the fundamental goal of the historic law: providing broad access to the disabled. Instead it seeks to reform what critics call confusing or restrictive mandates.

The most contentious issue was discipline. The bill would make it easier for schools to remove disabled students from the classroom if they posed a threat to themselves or others. But it does not allow a cut-off of educational services in severe cases, as some lawmakers wanted.
It would gradually change the federal funding formula to reduce what critics said were incentives for schools to identify students as disabled.

To avoid expensive court fights, states would have to offer mediation to resolve disputes between parents and schools. Parents would have more opportunity to be involved in decisions about a child's placement but would face new requirements before moving children to private education.

"(This) will have a real and positive impact on the lives of millions of students," Education Committee Chairman William Goodling, a Pennsylvania Republican, said. "These changes will mean more time for teachers to dedicate to their students and fewer resources wasted on process."
President Clinton, in a statement, praised the vote. "This legislation strengthens and reaffirms our commitment to these chidren and their parents and I look forward to signing it."
The 22-year-old IDEA law is credited with giving millions of children with physical, emotional and mental impairments entry to the public education system.
An estimated 5.4 million children are now guaranteed access to special equipment, teachers and programmes.

But schools complain Congress never met its commitment to help meet the expensive requirements of the law. Washington covers about nine percent of costs, far below a 40 percent goal. There have been concerns the law is overly restrictive.
Lawmakers last year tried to work out a deal to rewrite the law, but failed. This time, under the direction of Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, they came to broad consensus.

"What we strove to achieve and what I believe we accomplished is a bill that protects the rights of children with disabilites and at the same time, fosters cooperation between parents, teachers (and) school boards," California Democratic Representative George Miller said.
Schools now operate under a patchwork of policies and court decisions as they try to address the controversial issue of discipline for disabled children.

Under the compromise bill, a disabled student who brought weapons or illegal drugs to school could be removed for up to 45 days while his case was considered. Schools now can take such action only if a student brings a gun.
A hearing officer, not a court, could decide if a child should be moved to another school or classroom.

In general, the bill would let schools discipline disabled students in the same manner as other children so long as the behaviour at question was not related to their impairment. But they could not cut off educational aid.

The bill keeps current funding formulas intact until Congress increases spending to more than $4.9 billion a year. At that point, a new formula would kick in allocating money based on an area's school-age population and poverty rate.
The current formula is based on the number of disabled children in a school district.
